questions.question: Which statement best describes what a Java String is?
options: An object that holds a sequence of characters
A primitive type, like `int` or `char`
A fixed-size array of `char` that you index with square brackets
A keyword that reserves memory for text but has no methods
questions.explanation: `String` is a class, so every string is an object with methods; primitives like `int` store bare values. The characters live inside the object - the variable itself only holds a reference to it.

questions.question: `String` can be used in any Java file without an `import` statement. Why?
options: The compiler replaces strings with `char` arrays, so no class is involved
`String` belongs to `java.lang`, which is imported automatically
`String` is a primitive type, and primitives never need imports
Any class whose name starts with a capital letter is imported automatically
questions.explanation: `String` lives in the `java.lang` package, the one package every Java file imports for free. It is a normal class - capital S, full method set - not a primitive.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: HELLO
Hello
hello
Nothing - it fails to compile because the return value of `toUpperCase()` is not used
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable: `toUpperCase()` builds and returns a new "HELLO" object, but nothing captures it, so `s` still points at "hello". Ignoring a return value is perfectly legal, so the code compiles and runs.

questions.question: You want to test whether two String variables hold exactly the same characters. Which expression is correct?
options: `s1.length() == s2.length()`
`s1.equals(s2)`
questions.explanation: `equals()` compares the actual text, character by character. `==` only asks whether both variables point at the same object - it can be false for identical text - and equal lengths prove nothing about the contents.

questions.question: Two variables are assigned the same literal: `String s1 = "Java";` and `String s2 = "Java";`. How many String objects hold that text?
options: One - both variables share the same object from the String pool
Two - every assignment creates its own object
Two at first, then the garbage collector merges them into one
Zero - literals are compiled into the code and never become objects
questions.explanation: The JVM keeps literals in the String pool and recycles them: the second "Java" literal reuses the object the first one created, so both variables point at one shared object. That sharing is safe precisely because no code can ever modify a String.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: 4 then J
5 then J
4 then a
3 then v
questions.explanation: `length()` counts the characters - four in "Java". Indexing starts at zero, so `charAt(0)` returns the first character, 'J'.

questions.question: What is the key difference between `String` and `StringBuilder`?
options: `String` stores only letters and digits; `StringBuilder` accepts any characters
A `String` can never be changed after creation, while a `StringBuilder` edits its contents in place
`StringBuilder` is thread-safe; `String` is not
`String` objects live in the heap; `StringBuilder` objects live in the String pool
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable - every apparent change manufactures a new object - while StringBuilder is a mutable character sequence whose methods modify the same object. The thread-safety distractor is backwards: String is safe because it cannot change, and StringBuilder is the unsynchronized one.

questions.question: When you call a "modifying" String method such as `trim()` or `replace()`, what actually happens?
options: The characters inside the original object are overwritten
The original object is destroyed and rebuilt with the new text
A brand-new String holding the result is created and returned; the original is untouched
Nothing at all, unless the String was created with `new`
questions.explanation: String methods are factories: they return a new String containing the result and leave the original exactly as it was. If you do not capture the returned reference, the result is lost.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: hello then 5
hello world then 11
hello then 11
hello world then 5
questions.explanation: `append()` edits the builder itself - no reassignment needed - so `sb` genuinely grows to "hello world", which is 11 characters counting the space. In-place mutation is exactly what StringBuilder exists for.

questions.question: What does this code print, in order?
options: true, true, true
false, false, true
true, false, true
true, false, false
questions.explanation: The two literals share one pooled object, so `a == b` is true. `new String(...)` always builds a fresh object even when an identical String sits in the pool, so `a == c` compares different objects and is false, while `equals()` reads the matching characters and says true.

questions.question: Code that compares Strings with `==` often passes its tests but fails with real input. What explains this?
options: `==` is slower than `equals()`, so comparisons time out on production data
Literals in tests share pooled objects, so `==` happens to be true; text read at run time is not pooled, so `==` is false even for matching text
`==` compares only the first character of each String
The String pool is disabled outside of test runs, so literals stop matching
questions.explanation: `==` compares references, and identical literals happen to point at one pooled object, so tests written with literals pass by luck. Strings that arrive at run time - typed by a user, read from a file, split from a line - are separate objects, so the same comparison quietly returns false. Always compare text with `equals()`.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: ha! then ha!
ha then ha
ha! then ha
It does not compile - `b` cannot be assigned from another String variable
questions.explanation: `b = a` copies the reference, so both variables point at "ha". The concatenation builds a new String "ha!" and moves only `a` to it; the shared original cannot have changed, so `b` still prints ha.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of String immutability?
options: Strings can be shared safely between threads without synchronization
A String's hash code can be computed once and cached
The String pool can let many variables share one object safely
Text can be appended repeatedly in a loop without creating extra objects
questions.explanation: Safe sharing, pooling, and hash-code caching all follow from the guarantee that a String can never change. Repeated appending is the cost side: because the object cannot grow, every concatenation must build a new String - the very problem StringBuilder solves.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: hello world
olleh
world hello
dlrow olleh
questions.explanation: Both calls edit the same object in place: `append` makes "hello world", then `reverse` flips the entire sequence to "dlrow olleh". Nothing needs to be caught or reassigned because StringBuilder is mutable.

questions.question: A loop runs 1000 times and each iteration executes `result += "x";` on a String variable. Roughly how many String objects does the loop create?
options: About 1000 - each `+=` builds a new String and abandons the previous one
One - the same String is extended each time
Two - one before the loop and one after it
Zero - the compiler folds the whole loop into a single constant
questions.explanation: A String cannot be extended, so every `+=` copies everything built so far into a brand-new object, leaving the old one as garbage - roughly one new String per iteration. A StringBuilder would edit one object for the entire loop.

questions.question: Which class gives you a mutable character sequence that several threads can safely modify at the same time?
options: `String`
`StringBuilder`
`char[]`
`StringBuffer`
questions.explanation: `StringBuffer`'s methods are synchronized, so threads cannot corrupt it mid-edit - that locking is also why it is slower. `StringBuilder` has the same API without locks, and `String` is thread-safe only because it cannot be modified at all.

questions.question: `StringBuffer` had existed since Java 1.0. Why did Java 5 add `StringBuilder`?
options: To provide the same API without synchronization, which is faster for the common single-threaded case
To add methods like `append()` and `insert()` that `StringBuffer` lacked
To make string building thread-safe for the first time
To replace the `String` class, which was being deprecated
questions.explanation: Every `StringBuffer` method takes a lock, and most code is single-threaded - paying for protection it never uses. `StringBuilder` is the same API with the locking removed, so it is noticeably faster; reach for `StringBuffer` only when threads genuinely share the object.

questions.question: The string below has two spaces on each side of the word. What does this code print?
options: Nothing - it fails to compile because `trim()`'s result is discarded
questions.explanation: `trim()` returns a new trimmed String, but the result is never assigned, so `s` still holds all eight characters - two spaces, Java, two spaces. Reassigning with `s = s.trim();` would make the length 4.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `replaceAll` treats its first argument as a regular expression, and the regex `.` matches any single character - so all five characters become dashes. For a literal replacement use `replace(".", "-")`, which prints 1-2-3.

questions.question: `String constructed = new String("Lab");` creates an object outside the String pool. What does `constructed.intern()` return?
options: The exact object `constructed` already points at
A second fresh copy of "Lab", also outside the pool
`null`, because Strings made with `new` can never be pooled
The pooled "Lab" object - so comparing the result to the literal "Lab" with `==` gives true
questions.explanation: `intern()` looks the content up in the String pool and returns the pooled object holding those characters. It only returns that reference - `constructed` keeps pointing at the heap object unless you reassign it, as in `constructed = constructed.intern();`.

questions.question: You have finished assembling text in a `StringBuilder` and must pass the result to a method that expects a `String`. What is the correct move?
options: Pass the builder directly - `StringBuilder` is a subclass of `String`
Call `toString()` on the builder to get a String holding its contents
Cast it: `(String) builder`
Call `append("")`, which converts the builder into a String
questions.explanation: A StringBuilder is not a String and cannot be cast to one - they are unrelated classes. `toString()` produces an immutable String snapshot of the builder's current contents: build in the builder, finish with `toString()`.

questions.question: In which situation should you switch from the `+` operator to a `StringBuilder`?
options: Joining two names once: `String full = first + " " + last;`
Printing a label: `System.out.println("Total: " + total);`
Appending one more piece to a result variable inside a loop with thousands of iterations
Concatenating three literals in a single expression on one line
questions.explanation: A lone `+` expression is fine - the compiler turns it into efficient building for you. The trouble is `+` repeated across loop iterations: each pass creates a new String from everything so far, which is exactly the workload StringBuilder eliminates.

questions.question: Why does the chained call `sb.append("a").append("b").append("c")` work on a `StringBuilder`?
options: `append()` returns the same builder it just modified, so each call feeds the next
`append()` returns a new StringBuilder each time, and the chain collects them
The compiler rewrites the chain into a single String concatenation
`StringBuilder` overloads the dot operator to allow chaining
questions.explanation: `append()` mutates the builder and then returns that same object, giving the next `.append()` something to act on. The whole chain is one builder edited three times - no new objects along the way.

questions.question: The variable `text` may be `null`. Which condition safely evaluates whether it contains "ok" without ever throwing a `NullPointerException`?
options: `text != null && text.contains("ok")`
`text.contains("ok") && text != null`
`text.contains("ok")` on its own - `contains()` simply returns false when `text` is null
`text == "ok"`
questions.explanation: `&&` evaluates left to right and stops as soon as the answer is known, so the null check must come first; when `text` is null the `contains()` call never runs. Reversing the order calls a method on null before the check and throws immediately, and `==` never throws but compares references rather than content.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: ABC: Java Strings!
Java Strings!
Strings!
ABC: Java!
questions.explanation: `append` gives "Java Strings!" and `insert(0, "ABC: ")` gives "ABC: Java Strings!". `delete(0, 5)` uses a half-open range - it removes indexes 0 through 4, exactly the five characters of "ABC: " - landing back on "Java Strings!", with every call editing the same object.

questions.question: What happens when you try to compile and run this code?
options: It prints 4
It prints 3
It fails to compile - `length` on a String is a method and needs parentheses
It compiles, but throws an exception at run time
questions.explanation: Arrays expose `length` as a field with no brackets, but String provides `length()` as a method - `s.length` without parentheses is not a member of String, so the compiler rejects the line. With `s.length()` it would print 4.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
options: It prints Java, then throws a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`
It prints Java, then prints a
The `substring` call throws, because index 4 is past the last character
It does not compile
questions.explanation: `substring`'s end index is exclusive, so it may equal the length - `substring(0, 4)` happily returns "Java". `charAt` has no such allowance: valid indexes run 0 to `length() - 1` (0 to 3 here), so `charAt(4)` throws at run time.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: Hello
hello
Hell
hell
questions.explanation: `setCharAt(0, 'h')` overwrites the first character in place, giving "hello"; `deleteCharAt(4)` then removes the 'o' at index 4, leaving "hell". Both calls mutate the one builder directly - no return values needed.

questions.question: Building an N-character string with `+=` in a loop does work proportional to N squared, not N. What causes the square law?
options: The garbage collector pauses the loop after every concatenation
Each `+=` must copy every character built so far into a new String before appending the new piece
The String pool is searched for every intermediate result
The hash code of the whole string is recomputed on every iteration
questions.explanation: Immutability means `+=` can never extend the existing String - it copies the entire text so far into a fresh object each time. Copying 1 + 2 + ... + N characters totals about N*N/2 work, which is how 10,000 appends end up copying on the order of 100 million characters.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: Hello then Hello
Hello World then Hello World
It does not compile - `substring` on a StringBuilder cannot be assigned to a String
Hello then Hello World
questions.explanation: Unusually for a StringBuilder method, `substring()` does not mutate: it returns a new String copy of the half-open range 0 to 5 and leaves the builder untouched. So `s` is "Hello" while `sb` still holds "Hello World".

questions.question: After this code runs, what is true of `r`?
options: `r` is positive, because "Kotlin" is the longer string
It does not compile - `compareTo` returns a `boolean`, not an `int`
`r` is negative, because "Java" orders alphabetically before "Kotlin"
`r` is 0, because `compareTo` tests reference equality and these are different objects
questions.explanation: `compareTo` compares lexicographically and returns an `int`: negative when the receiver sorts first, zero for equal content, positive when it sorts after. 'J' comes before 'K', so `"Java".compareTo("Kotlin")` is negative.

questions.question: Which single call joins the array `{"Java", "Strings", "are", "powerful"}` into "Java Strings are powerful"?
options: `String.join(words, " ")` - array first, then the separator
`String.format(" ", words)`
`words.join(" ")`
`String.join(" ", words)` - separator first, then the array
questions.explanation: `String.join` takes the separator as its first argument followed by the pieces, and returns them joined with the separator between each pair - no loop required. Arrays have no `join` method of their own, and `String.format` fills placeholders in a template instead.
